title: Collocation and register
summary: Select a word or phrase that expresses the intended meaning, forms a natural partnership and matches the formality of the situation.

sections.title: Correct words still need to belong together
content: English words often prefer particular partners. We make a decision, reach a decision or take a decision in some varieties of English, but we do not perform a decision. Meaning alone cannot settle the choice.
The same message can also change with the situation. ‘Let me know’ suits a message to a friend; ‘please notify the office’ suits a formal instruction. Neither level of formality is always better.

sections.title: Use Meaning, Partnership, Audience and Sentence
content: Meaning: predict the precise idea needed before looking at the options.
Partnership: test which words normally combine in that grammatical frame. A familiar word can still create an unnatural collocation.
Audience: identify who is communicating, to whom and for what purpose. Choose formal, neutral or informal language to fit that relationship—not to sound artificially impressive.
Sentence: insert the whole option and reread. Check grammar, required prepositions, meaning and tone together.

sections.title: Match the partnership and the situation
content: Consider a school notice: ‘The revised safety rules will take effect on Monday.’ The meaning is that the rules begin to operate. ‘Take effect’ is the natural partnership in a neutral-formal notice.

‘Do effect’ and ‘make effect’ use common verbs but do not form this expression. ‘Kick in’ can express a similar beginning in informal conversation, yet it is less suitable for the notice. The best choice passes both the partnership and audience checks.
Register is not a contest for the longest word. Clear neutral language is often more appropriate than either slang or inflated formality.

sections.title: Test the frame aloud
content: For two items, predict the meaning, read the words around the blank as one frame and name the communication setting. Eliminate an option only with a specific reason: unnatural partnership, missing grammar or unsuitable register.

sections.title: Choose natural language, not decorative language
content: On three unseen items, check the fixed or common partnership before comparing how formal the options sound. Then use the named report, notice or personal message to settle the register.
Reject dramatic language when the evidence is measured, and reject inflated language when a simple conversational phrase communicates more naturally.

sections.title: Name the earliest failed check
content: Meaning mismatch: the option says something different. Partnership error: the words do not naturally combine in this frame. Grammar-frame error: a required preposition or form is missing. Register mismatch: the wording is too casual, too formal or unnecessarily dramatic for the audience.
Record the earliest failure and repair it explicitly: ‘X has the intended meaning, but Y is the natural partnership here’ or ‘Both are understandable, but X fits this audience.’

sections.title: Transfer all four checks
content: Complete one unseen formal-context decision without labelled support. A failed or hinted attempt enters the retry queue with a different sentence and collocation rather than repeating the exposed wording.
